Neat project, but speaking as a multigenerational pneumatic conveyor systems engineer (focusing on fabrication and airflow dynamics), there are serious issues here: massive turbulence, flow restrictions, and incorrect input-to-output dynamics indicated by the fan blade pitch.

​Edit: There is also severe airborne particulate contamination due to zero filtration or enclosure. At least add some filter screens to the fans. Beyond that, using identical fans throughout without an independent fan controller creates major volumetric balancing problems.

"4x RTX 5090, 32GB VRAM each, 128GB in total."  
Yes, 128GB in total but does your local agent see it as one 128GB or 4 cards, each 32GB? To my knowledge, there is no NVLink etc for retail consumer cards (after RTX 3090); can you clarify how you tackled this if you did?

yup you're right, these 4 cards don't behave like one 128GB GPU. It's four separate 32GB pools talking over PCIe 5.0 x16, not one 128GB pool.

What makes a model bigger than 32GB run anyway is tensor parallel in vLLM: the weights get sharded across the four cards and every token does an all-reduce between them over PCIe. It works, and it's what every multi-GPU consumer rig does now, but it isn't free. PCIe all-reduce is slower than NVLink would be, so you pay a sync tax that grows the more you shard.

So it's best when the model you pick fit comfortably and you're running it to server a team, where the win is aggregate bandwidth. If someone needs one huge model with minimal sharding, fewer cards with more VRAM each is the better shape, which is why we also build a 2x 96GB (Dual RTX PRO 6000)

Why not use an RTX 6000 instead of 4 gpu without nvlink?

well, the 1st reason is **total VRAM per dollar**. You may check you local retailer and calculate how much VRAM/USD each one would give you and see what I'm talking about.

In local LLMs, VRAM determines which models you can actually load. With 48GB, you cannot run large 70B models at high context, but 96GB+ (or 128GB like 4x 5090) handles them easily.

Missing NVLink is not a dealbreaker for inference either. Token generation speed is mostly limited by each card's internal memory bandwidth, not PCIe bus speed. Standard PCIe 4.0 or 5.0 slots provide plenty of bandwidth for tools like vLLM or llama.cpp to split the workload.

Four separate cards also let you run multiple independent models at the same time with zero interference, while a single RTX 6000 forces every job into one queue.

You only pick the RTX 6000 if you want a personal compact build with low power draw and simple setup. If raw capacity and multi-tasking matter, 4 GPUs win easily.
